In 1892, in the town of Necochea in Argentina, police solved a murder by matching a bloody fingerprint, the first known case of its kind. It made Argentina the first country to identify criminals by their fingerprints.

The case was the killing of two young children. Their mother, Francisca Rojas, blamed a neighbour. An inspector found a bloody thumb mark on a door frame and compared it with prints of the suspects, using the method of Juan Vucetich, a Croatian-born police official in La Plata. The print matched the mother, who then confessed.

Scientists in Britain, notably Francis Galton, had shown that fingerprints are unique and do not change. Vucetich built a practical way to file and search them, which he called dactyloscopy. Argentina's police adopted it, and it spread through Latin America. Britain and India used a rival system developed by Edward Henry. Fingerprints soon replaced the older method of body measurements and became the basis of modern forensic identification.
sum: In 1892, in the town of Necochea in Argentina, police solved a murder by matching a bloody fingerprint, the first known case of its kind. It made Argentina the first country to identify criminals by their fingerprints.
